Owner Takes His Ford Mustang Dark Horse to a Tuner, Goes Home With GTD Power
17 photos
Photo: Late Model Racecraft | YouTube
Why pay over $350,000 for the Ford Mustang GTD when a tuner can give you GTD power on a Mustang Dark Horse for a fraction of the price? This is what the owner of this muscle car must have thought the moment he drove to a tuner in Houston, Texas. A couple of weeks later, he went home with 800 horsepower. Nope! No turbos involved in this build!
Some car guys don't do stock. Factory specification just doesn't cut it for them. Take the owner of this 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse . A short while ago, he drove home in his brand-new Mustang Dark Horse, powered by the 5.0-liter Coyote V8 with naturally aspirated firepower.
The V8 pumped out 500 horsepower (507 metric horsepower) and 418 pound-feet (567 Newton meters) of torque for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 4.1 seconds and a top speed of 166 mph (267 kph) when equipped with the ten-speed automatic transmission, like this car is.
The owner wanted to take the Mustang Dark Horse to the next level. So now, he can beat the hell out of his brand-new toy, with no compromise on reliability and driveability. It is still a perfect daily driver, without turning violent.
Photo: Late Model Racecraft | YouTube An aftermarket Magnuson TVS2650 supercharger, the same one that the tuners use on many General Motors' cars like the Chevrolet Corvettes and Camaros, added over 250 rear-wheel horsepower. But how did they get that far?
They came up with an extra expansion tank to keep things cool under the hood. An extra intercooler pump made its way into the engine bay, along with a new heat exchanger. The factory air box remained, and so did the headers, exhaust, and fuel system. The car still drives on pump gas and comes with a factory-style warranty offered by the tuner.
The Mustang Dark Horse drove into the shop making 421 rear-wheel horsepower and 353 pound-feet of rear-wheel torque and drove out making 676.7 rear-wheel horsepower and 537.8 pound-feet of rear-wheel torque. That’s a solid 256 rear-wheel horsepower and 185 pound-feet of rear-wheel torque.
That would be roughly 800 horsepower and 635 pound-feet at the crank. In the meantime, the most powerful road-going Mustang, the GTD, comes with 815 horsepower (826 metric horsepower) and 664 pound-feet (900 Newton meters) of torque for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.7 seconds and a top speed of 202 mph (325 kph).
Photo: Late Model Racecraft | YouTube The tuner can squeeze more out of the 5.0-liter V8 in case the owner comes back for more. So why buy a Mustang GTD when a dialed-up Dark Horse can do nearly just as good?
Now, Steven Fereday of Late Model Racecraft took the Mustang Dark Horse out for a spin to make sure that it runs, drives, shifts, and behaves properly with the massive power gain that it will go home with.
The car blows the tires off in first gear with traction control off and grabs the second gear to regain grip and takes off the line like there is no tomorrow, gluing the driver into the seat, delivering torque right from the get-go.
The Ford Mustang Dark Horse starts at $70,570, while the Mustang GTD is a $350,000 deal before adding fees and options. Late Model Racecraft does not disclose the price of the upgrade, but it is surely far under the price of the GTD, even though it brings nearly as much power.
